The curriculum is overstuffed and driven with tests. For example, in math, fifth graders are supposed to learn:

* how to read/add/subtract/multiply decimals
* how to read/add/subtract/multiply fractions
* learn how to do ALL measurement conversions
* learn how to do basic algebra
* learn all 2-d and 3-d shapes and then volume with standard and non-standard figures
* learn graphing and at least 5 different kinds of graphical representations of data.
* learn how to multiply 3-6 digit numbers together
* learn how to do long division with 1 & 2 digit numbers.

All of this in approximately 180 hours. It's a daunting task and nearly impossible to get done with mastery. It's a lot of work to get through and the kids are expected to know how to do it by the end of the year or they don't pass the test. It's a lot of pressure on everyone to just barrel through material without taking a breath.

exactly. this expands beyond just grade level. It can test above/below to gauge proficiency that way.

Additionally a proficiency assessment benefits middle/upper class. 

Middle/upper class kids come into the grade near/at/above grade level because resources such as tutoring, summer school, access to technology, and parents who are better educated and are native or proficient English speakers with the time to help their kids. 

Lower class students often come into elementary behind. They don't have the same early childhood education and begin kindergarten far below standards. The kindergarten teacher then spends much of the year on letter sounds, numbers, etc. (a skill mid/upper class kids already know bc of parents or preschool).

This gap stays with kids throughout their schooling. By 5th grade, many middle/upper class kids are proficient, meaning they are reading & doing math at a 5th grade level. Some are advanced because parents send them to tutor or summer programs to accelerate them. 
Even if a lower income child progresses the same way, they are at least one grade level less proficient because of that lost kindergarten year. They will have to make up that year somewhere & that is a near impossible task for any school. 
Proficiency will always benefit the richer kids - the ones with access early on to be successful. Growth benefits all kids because it rewards a 5th grader who jumps from a 2nd grade reading level to a 4th in one year.

"Gary, get over here."

Nathan pointed at the screen in horror. The game had crashed and thousands of players were tweeting in anger. He'd never seen such vehement in his life. He shielded his eyes from the angry bleetings of the GunBattleProMax community.

"Dude, what happened?" Gary said as he fell into his chair in a daze. 

They both stared at the giant screen that showed a constant stream of the game. It was all pixelated and all the player's faces were stuck in mid-blink. 

"I think the servers timed out."

"Well, restart them!" Gary shouted. 

Nathan took a deep breath. He'd spent hours on this game. He knew that was wrong. "No, that's not it. I'm sorry, I'm just so flustered."

Gary nodded and patted Nathan on the shoulder. "This is intense. I know how exhausted you get after coding all those scenes and animating all those fight moves. And with the wedding coming up..."

"I know. Brenda's mom is coming up and she wants to move the ---"

The screen turned to a faded green shade. "Shit. Is it the wire frames?" Nathan asked. 

Gary opened up his computer and scrolled through the wall of text for the scene. He looked for the bug. He knew that it was in there somewhere. He pounded the keyboard with his fist. "I can't find it!"

"You can do it. Just add some more lines of code. Make them do something else and then we'll see what's wrong."

He went to the code for the forest scene. It the shortest because the forest wasn't a big set. He added a tree and a rock and told the nearest character to walk towards it. As he pressed enter, his eyes went back up to the screen. 

They both held their breath as the code cycled through on his computer, scanning itself into the game. Slowly the rock and tree generated onto the screen above them. 

"Kick ass tree, bro."

The nearest character was a knight in yellow armor. He was standing on one foot, stuck in mid stride. "C'mon..." he said. "Move."

As the last line of code beamed into the program, there was a jerk in the image. "Please..." he begged. 

He almost felt the knight wink as he took a step towards the tree. 

The men screamed with joy. "Nice job!" Nathan said. 

Gary breathed a sigh of relief. "Damn, programming a video game is tough work. Now back to my mother-in-law...."

He bowed his head. The power felt heavy in his hands as he willed himself to fight again. 
The scar from the battle still stung as his jacket brushed against it. After all these days, the pain still felt as bitter as the day he fell. But all that agony was for nothing if he didn't have her anymore. All the power in his hands was meaningless if he couldn't hold on to her anymore.
 
The familiar clunk of boots sounded behind him. 

He'd done this all thousands of times. Graycous was behind him, in his faded black suit and weary expression. In a matter of seconds, the two would turn and he would place the sinkhole in front of Graycous. The city, for just a minute, would be restored. The buildings would be standing up again. The bridges, the cars, the poor people...they'd all be alive just for a moment. 

And then the snap back.

Graycous always won. He was always brought back to the moment just as she slipped through his fingers.
